title: Exploitation for Client Execution
summary: Exploitation for client execution is the abuse of a software flaw in an application that the victim runs locally, in order to obtain code execution in that application's context. The targets are the programs people use constantly: browsers and their rendering engines, office and productivity suites, document readers, media players, messaging clients and chat add-ons. The delivery path differs by target. Browsers are reached through drive-by compromise or a malicious link, and the exploit may fire without any further click once the page loads. Office documents and other file formats arrive as attachments or download links and need the victim to open them. In every case the adversary sends crafted data that the application parses incorrectly, and control flow is redirected inside a process the user already trusts. Detection rarely involves spotting the exploit itself, because the payload is memory resident. Analysts work from crash and hang reports, exploit mitigation events such as Data Execution Prevention or Control Flow Guard trips, a document reader or office process spawning a shell or downloader, the process contacting an unfamiliar destination immediately after handling a file, and the file's origin in mail or browser download records.

beginner.definition: This means an attacker uses a bug in a program you already use to run their code. The program might be a web browser or a document reader. You may only need to open a file or visit a page. The attacker's code then runs as if it were part of that program.
beginner.whyItMatters: You use these programs every day, so their traffic and files look normal. The attacker does not need to trick you into running a strange program. In some cases you do not even have to click, because loading the page is enough. A successful exploit gives the attacker a foothold on your computer.
howItWorks: The attacker finds a bug in an application that many people use, such as a browser or an office program.
They build a file or a web page that the program will read incorrectly and then follow their instructions.
The file or link is delivered by email, a message, or a website the victim visits.
The victim opens the file, or in a browser case simply loads the page.
The program mishandles the crafted data, and the attacker's code runs inside that program.
That code then downloads tools and starts the next stage of the intrusion.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk where staff open any envelope marked urgent. Someone posts an envelope with a fold that jams the letter opener in a special way. While the clerk fights the jam, a second person slips behind the desk. Nobody attacked the clerk and the envelope looked ordinary, but the tool did something it was never designed to do.
takeaways: Keep browsers, office suites and document readers patched, because these are the usual targets.
Treat unexpected crashes in these programs as possible exploit attempts, not just bad luck.
A document reader or browser that starts a shell or downloader is a serious warning sign.

objectives: Explain how a software vulnerability in a client application leads to code execution.
Compare browser based exploitation with document based exploitation and their user actions.
Describe why memory resident exploitation leaves little file based evidence.
Identify crash reports, exploit mitigation events and suspicious child processes as detection sources.
Explain why prompt patching of browsers, office suites and document readers reduces this risk.
